bodyText:
What is a DBMS?

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that stores, organizes, retrieves and manages data in a structured way. A database is an organized collection of related data, and the DBMS acts as an interface between the users and the database, allowing users to create, read, update and delete data without knowing how it is physically stored.

Before DBMS, data was kept in separate files (the file system approach), which caused duplication, inconsistency and difficult access. A DBMS removes these problems by storing data centrally and controlling access to it.

Components of a DBMS

  • Hardware: the physical computer system on which the database runs.
  • Software: the DBMS itself, for example MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
  • Data: the actual facts stored in the database.
  • Users: the Database Administrator (DBA), application programmers and end users.
  • Procedures: the rules and instructions for using and managing the database.

The Three-Schema Architecture

The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture divides a database into three levels. The external level is how individual users view the data. The conceptual level describes the whole database structure, including all tables and relationships. The internal level describes how data is physically stored on disk. This separation gives data independence: physical data independence means changing storage does not affect the conceptual design, and logical data independence means changing the conceptual design does not disturb user views.

Advantages of a DBMS

  • Reduces data redundancy (duplication) and therefore data inconsistency.
  • Provides controlled, concurrent access so many users can work at the same time.
  • Enforces data integrity and security through rules and permissions.
  • Offers backup and recovery in case of failure.
  • Provides data independence between the application programs and the stored data.
keyPoints: DBMS stands for Database Management System.
A database is an organized collection of related data.
The DBA (Database Administrator) is responsible for managing and securing the database.
The ANSI/SPARC three-schema architecture was proposed in 1975.
The three levels are external, conceptual and internal.
Physical data independence means changing physical storage does not affect the conceptual schema.
Logical data independence means changing the conceptual schema does not affect user views.
Data redundancy means unnecessary duplication of the same data.
A DBMS provides concurrent access, allowing many users to use the database at the same time.
Popular DBMS examples are MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL.
The file system approach suffered from data isolation, duplication and inconsistency.
Data integrity means the accuracy and consistency of stored data.

bodyText:
The Relational Model

The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970 in his paper 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'. In this model, data is stored in tables called relations. Each table has rows, called tuples, and columns, called attributes. Each attribute has a domain, which is the set of permitted values for that column. The number of attributes is called the degree of the relation, and the number of tuples is called its cardinality.

The ER Model

The Entity-Relationship (ER) model was introduced by Peter Chen in 1976 and is used to design a database before it is built. An entity is a real-world object, such as Student or Book. An attribute is a property of an entity, such as a student's name. Attributes may be simple, composite (made of parts, like a full name), multivalued (such as phone numbers) or derived (calculated from others, such as age from date of birth). A relationship describes how entities are connected.

Cardinality and Participation

Cardinality describes how many entities on one side relate to the other side: one-to-one (1:1), one-to-many (1:N) and many-to-many (M:N). Participation may be total, meaning every entity must take part in the relationship, or partial, meaning participation is optional. A weak entity cannot exist on its own and depends on a strong entity, for example a loan payment depends on the loan.

ER Diagram Symbols

In an ER diagram, rectangles represent entities, ellipses represent attributes, diamonds represent relationships, and lines connect them. A double rectangle shows a weak entity and a double line shows total participation.

bodyText:
What is SQL?

SQL stands for Structured Query Language. It is the standard language for working with relational databases. It was developed at IBM in the 1970s for the System R project and was originally called SEQUEL (Structured English Query Language). SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987.

Categories of SQL Commands

SQL commands fall into groups. Data Definition Language (DDL) commands such as CREATE, ALTER and DROP define the structure of the database. Data Manipulation Language (DML) commands such as SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE work with the data itself. Data Control Language (DCL) commands such as GRANT and REVOKE control permissions, and Transaction Control Language (TCL) commands such as COMMIT and ROLLBACK manage transactions.

The Four Core DML Statements

  • SELECT retrieves data: SELECT name, marks FROM Students WHERE marks > 80 ORDER BY marks DESC;
  • INSERT adds new rows: INSERT INTO Students (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Ali');
  • UPDATE changes existing rows: UPDATE Students SET marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;
  • DELETE removes rows: DELETE FROM Students WHERE id = 1;

The WHERE clause filters rows, ORDER BY sorts the result, DISTINCT removes duplicate values, and aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarize data. GROUP BY groups rows and HAVING filters groups.

ORDER BY sorts query results in ascending or descending order.
DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result.
COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX are aggregate functions in SQL.

bodyText:
Why Keys Matter

Keys are attributes, or combinations of attributes, that identify rows in a table and link tables together. Without keys, a database could not guarantee that each row is unique or that relationships between tables stay correct.

Types of Keys

  • Super key: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a tuple. Every table has at least one super key.
  • Candidate key: a minimal super key, meaning no attribute can be removed from it without losing uniqueness.
  • Primary key: the candidate key chosen by the designer as the main identifier of the table. It must be unique and can never contain a NULL value.
  • Alternate key: a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.
  • Foreign key: an attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table. It creates the relationship between the two tables.
  • Composite key: a key made of two or more attributes together.
  • Surrogate key: an artificial key generated by the system, such as an auto-increment ID, used when no natural attribute is suitable.

Referential Integrity

Referential integrity is the rule that a foreign key value must either match an existing primary key value in the referenced table or be NULL. It prevents orphan records, for example an order that refers to a customer who does not exist.

bodyText:
Why Normalize?

Normalization is the process of organizing data in a database to reduce redundancy and remove insertion, deletion and update anomalies. An insertion anomaly means new data cannot be added without other data. A deletion anomaly means deleting one fact accidentally deletes another. An update anomaly means the same fact must be changed in several places, risking inconsistency. Normalization works by splitting tables and is guided by functional dependencies: a dependency X to Y means the value of X determines the value of Y.

The Normal Forms

  • First Normal Form (1NF): every attribute must hold atomic (indivisible) values, and there must be no repeating groups. Each cell holds a single value.
  • Second Normal Form (2NF): the table must be in 1NF, and every non-key attribute must depend on the whole primary key, not just part of it. 2NF removes partial dependency, which can only occur when the primary key is composite.
  • Third Normal Form (3NF): the table must be in 2NF, and no non-key attribute may depend on another non-key attribute. 3NF removes transitive dependency.

Beyond 3NF lies Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF), a stronger version of 3NF proposed by Raymond Boyce and E. F. Codd in 1974. The opposite of normalization is denormalization, which deliberately reintroduces redundancy to improve read performance.
keyPoints: Normalization is the process of organizing data to reduce redundancy.
An insertion anomaly means new data cannot be added without other data present.
A deletion anomaly means deleting one fact accidentally deletes another fact.
An update anomaly means the same fact must be changed in several places.
In First Normal Form (1NF), every attribute holds atomic values only.
1NF forbids repeating groups and multi-valued attributes in a single cell.
In Second Normal Form (2NF), there is no partial dependency on part of a composite key.
A table must be in 1NF before it can be in 2NF.
In Third Normal Form (3NF), there is no transitive dependency between non-key attributes.
A table must be in 2NF before it can be in 3NF.
BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form) was proposed by Raymond Boyce and E. F. Codd in 1974.
Denormalization deliberately adds redundancy back to improve read performance.
